title: Fatigue & Failure Analysis
summary: S-N curves, endurance limit modifiers, Goodman and Miner cumulative damage for predicting and preventing fatigue failures.

sections.heading: Why Parts Fail Under Repeated Load
sections.content:
Most mechanical failures — roughly 80% of service fractures — are **fatigue**: failure under repeated stress far below the static yield strength. The damage accumulates invisibly: a crack nucleates at a stress concentration, grows one load cycle at a time, and finally propagates to sudden fracture. The part looks perfect one day and broken the next.

Fatigue analysis answers three questions: *Will it survive N cycles? How much margin? What governs?* — before production, not after field failure.

sections.heading: S-N Curves & the Endurance Limit
sections.content:
The **S-N (Wöhler) curve** plots cyclic stress amplitude vs cycles to failure on log scales. For **steels**, the curve flattens at a **knee** (~10⁶–10⁷ cycles for most engineering steels): below the **endurance limit** $S_e$, the part can cycle indefinitely. For steels:

$$S_e' \approx 0.5 \, S_{ut} \quad (S_{ut} < 1400 \text{ MPa})$$

- **Steels and titanium**: true endurance limit; design for infinite life below it.
- **Aluminium, magnesium, most non-ferrous**: **no** endurance limit — the curve keeps falling; design for a *finite* life at a specified cycle count.
- **Cast iron**: flake graphite blunts crack tips; endurance limit ~0.4 S_ut and, counterintuitively, **compressive preloads** from casting help.

$S_e'$ is the *idealized* rotating-beam value; the *actual* part endurance limit is much lower once all the modifiers below are applied.

sections.heading: Endurance Limit Modifiers
sections.content:
The part endurance limit multiplies a series of correction factors onto the ideal value:

$$S_e = k_a \, k_b \, k_c \, k_d \, k_e \, S_e'$$

with (typical values):

- **$k_a$ — surface finish**: machined 0.9, ground 0.95, hot-rolled 0.7, as-forged ~0.5. Surface roughness is where real parts lose fatigue life first.
- **$k_b$ — size**: larger sections have more defect probability: ~1.0 for d ≤ 8 mm, falling to ~0.85 at d = 50 mm (non-rotating loading scales differently).
- **$k_c$ — loading**: bending 1.0, axial 0.7, torsion 0.577 (the von Mises ratio for pure shear).
- **$k_d$ — temperature**: falls above ~350 °C; **$k_e$ — reliability**: 1.0 (50%) down to 0.70 (99.9%) via the normal-distribution z-score.

A machined, bent steel shaft rarely keeps more than ~30–40% of its ideal endurance limit — this is why catalog "material strength" numbers cannot be used as part design allowables.

sections.heading: Fluctuating Stress & Goodman
sections.content:
Real loads fluctuate between a minimum and maximum — decomposed into a **mean** $\sigma_m = (\sigma_{max}+\sigma_{min})/2$ and **amplitude** $\sigma_a = (\sigma_{max}-\sigma_{min})/2$. Mean stress is harmful: a tensile mean reduces the allowable amplitude. The **Goodman criterion**:

$$\frac{\sigma_a}{S_e} + \frac{\sigma_m}{S_{ut}} = \frac{1}{n}$$

Example — $\sigma_a = 80$ MPa, $\sigma_m = 120$ MPa, $S_e = 200$ MPa, $S_{ut} = 600$ MPa:

$$\frac{80}{200} + \frac{120}{600} = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = \frac{1}{0.6} = 1.67$$

Goodman is the **conservative** straight-line criterion; Gerber (parabolic) is closer to mean test data but less used for design. Note the practical lever: **compressive mean stress helps** (bolt preload, shot peening, interference fits) — one reason preloaded joints and peened surfaces outlive as-machined ones (see [[fasteners-and-threaded-joints|bolted joints]]).

sections.heading: Cumulative Damage (Miner)
sections.content:
Service loads rarely have one amplitude — they are a **spectrum** (startup, cruise, overloads). **Miner's rule** accumulates fractional damage:

$$\sum \frac{n_i}{N_i} \leq 1$$

where $n_i$ cycles applied at level $i$, and $N_i$ the life at that level from the S-N curve. Example block: 10⁴ cycles at a level good for 10⁵ (0.1), then 10³ at a level good for 10⁴ (0.1) → damage 0.2, remaining life fraction 0.8 at the continuing level.

Miner's caveats: damage fractions sum to ~1 only for **steels in the finite-life region**; below the endurance limit Miner says damage = 0 (true for clean steel), but corrosion and fretting create real damage below S_e; sequence effects (underload-overload interactions) can shift the rule either way. For safety-critical variable-load parts use **modified Miner with a safety margin (damage ≤ 0.5)** or switch to fracture mechanics.

sections.heading: Stress Concentrations & Notch Sensitivity
sections.content:
Fatigue cracks virtually always start at a **notch**: shoulder fillet, keyway, thread root, oil hole. The elastic stress concentration factor $K_t$ is geometry-defined (charts or FEA), but real materials do not feel the full theoretical peak. The **fatigue stress concentration factor**:

$$K_f = 1 + q(K_t - 1)$$

with **notch sensitivity** $q$ (0 = insensitive, 1 = fully sensitive). For steels, $q$ rises with hardness and notch radius — a fine thread in quenched steel feels nearly the full $K_t$; a sharp keyway corner in mild steel feels less. Practical consequences:

- **Generous fillet radii** ($r \geq 0.1\,d$ at shoulders) are the cheapest fatigue fix in design.
- Threads, keyways, and press-fit ends concentrate stress: relocate them out of the highest-bending zone or step the shaft.
- **Surface treatments** (shot peening, rolling, nitriding) put the surface in compression — losing $K_t$ sensitivity while gaining $S_e$.

Fatigue analysis software and the [[cae-analysis|CAE]] workflow apply exactly these rules in FEA: mesh the notch, extract $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_m$ per node, run Goodman, and flag the worst node as the governing fatigue location.

keyTakeaways: Steel has a true endurance limit ≈ 0.5·Sut; aluminium does not — size it for finite life.
Apply the full modifier stack (surface, size, loading, temperature, reliability) — ideal Se is never the part Se.
Goodman 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Sut catches mean-stress effects; compressive mean stress is your friend.
Miner accumulates spectrum damage; keep damage ≤ 0.5–1.0 and watch notches — Kf = 1 + q(Kt − 1).
